input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-519: Seminar in Computer Graphics. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: This course examines current topics in Computer Graphics. This is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Computer Graphics and Visualization cluster. Contact Hours: Lecture 3

Source excerpts:

[khronos-opengl]
The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages. Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles. Clipping removes portions outside the view volume. Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates. Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs. Fragment processing computes values for framebuffer operations. Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values. Blending combines a fragment result with an existing framebuffer value. Coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit.

[mit-computer-graphics]
Computer graphics uses geometric models to represent objects and scenes. Transformations position and orient geometry within coordinate systems. Viewing maps a scene through a camera model to an image. Rasterization samples projected primitives on a discrete pixel grid. Shading models how light, material, and geometry determine appearance. Texture mapping associates image data with geometric surfaces. Curves and surfaces provide compact smooth shape representations. Animation changes scene state over time. Ray tracing follows visibility and light paths through a scene. Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error.

Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Computer Graphics and Visualization cluster. Contact Hours: Lecture 3

beats.claim: The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages.
beats.example: Vertex attributes like position and normal are passed from the application to the vertex shader for initial transformation.
beats.title: Pipeline Foundation: Vertex Processing
beats.visualDirection: Display a flowchart showing vertices entering the vertex shader stage with labeled input/output attributes.

beats.claim: Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles.
beats.example: Three consecutive vertex indices are connected to form a triangle primitive that defines a planar surface.
beats.title: Primitive Assembly
beats.visualDirection: Show a wireframe triangle with numbered vertex indices and a line connecting them to a primitive assembly buffer.

beats.claim: Clipping removes portions outside the view volume.
beats.example: A triangle extending beyond the camera's frustum is clipped at the clipping plane boundaries.
beats.title: View Volume Clipping
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a 3D cube with a frustum overlay, highlighting clipped edges and the resulting clipped polygon.

beats.claim: Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates.
beats.example: Each triangle is subdivided into a set of pixels, generating a fragment for every covered pixel.
beats.title: Rasterization Conversion
beats.visualDirection: Show a subdivided triangle with a rasterization mask indicating which pixels are covered.

beats.claim: Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs.
beats.example: Color and normal values are linearly interpolated across the triangle to determine per-fragment properties.
beats.title: Interpolation Values
beats.visualDirection: Display a triangle with gradient shading showing interpolated color values moving from vertex to fragment.

beats.claim: Fragment processing computes values for framebuffer operations.
beats.example: The fragment shader calculates final color, alpha, and depth values for each pixel.
beats.title: Fragment Processing
beats.visualDirection: Show a fragment shader code snippet with labeled inputs and outputs mapping to framebuffer writes.

beats.claim: Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values.
beats.example: A fragment is discarded if its computed depth exceeds the stored depth value in the depth buffer.
beats.title: Depth Testing Visibility
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a depth buffer comparison with a foreground fragment passing and a background fragment failing.

beats.claim: Blending combines a fragment result with an existing framebuffer value.
beats.example: Alpha blending mixes the new fragment color with the existing pixel color using a specified blend factor.
beats.title: Blending Operations
beats.visualDirection: Show a split screen with a semi-transparent overlay blending onto a base image using a blend equation.

beats.claim: Coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit.
beats.example: Texture coordinates are explicitly mapped from object space to UV space to avoid sampling artifacts.
beats.title: Coordinate Spaces and Sampling
beats.visualDirection: Display a texture coordinate grid on a 3D surface with explicit UV mapping lines and sampling points.

beats.claim: Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error.
beats.example: A checklist verifies explicit coordinate mappings, proper sampling rates, and error bounds before rendering.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a checklist graphic with checkboxes for explicit conventions, sampling decisions, measurable error, and assumptions.

learningObjectives: Define the core stages of the OpenGL graphics pipeline and their sequential processing of vertex data.
Explain how geometric transformations, viewing models, and rasterization convert 3D scene representations into discrete pixel grids.
Evaluate visual correctness by identifying how explicit conventions, sampling decisions, and measurable error bounds determine final image output.
